We are pleased to present

Antisemitism and Antizionism After October 7.
The events of October 7, 2023, and the 
Gaza war that followed have transformed schol-
arly and public debate about Jews, Israel, and 
antisemitism. Questions that had long occupied 
scholars, policymakers, and communal organi -
sations have acquired renewed urgency: how 
should contemporary antisemitism be under -
stood and measured? What is the relationship 
between antisemitism and antizionism? How 
are attitudes toward Jews and Israel changing, 
particularly among younger generations? And 
what are the implications of these develop -
ments for law, politics, and public discourse? 
The contributions collected here address these 
questions from a variety of disciplinary perspec-
tives. Taken together, they offer new empirical 
evidence, conceptual analysis, legal argument, 
and critical reflection on some of the most con-
sequential debates surrounding antisemitism 
and antizionism in the post-October 7 era.

PROVO — The Utah County Clerk's Office inadvertently sent mailers to some registered voters incorrectly stating that they needed to return a copy of their ID with their mail-in ballot or it would be rejected.

Some first-time voters do need to include a copy of their ID when sending their ballot back, but the ID is not required with returned ballots if a voter has previously voted or has already verified their identity beforehand. The clerk's office sent out some 6,144 notices alerting voters of the need to include a copy of their ID ahead of this fall's midterms, but at least 71 went to people who had previously voted, and an unknown number were sent to first-time voters who had already been verified, according to Utah County Clerk Aaron Davidson.

He said a clerical error in his office led to the notices being sent out, but his team has fixed the issue, ensuring ballots will not be rejected for those who have already verified their identity.

"There's processes in place, but we're not going to disenfranchise anybody," he told KSL on Friday.

The Utah Elections Handbook requires election workers to verify identity when voters register by comparing it with a database containing driver's license numbers and Social Security numbers. If a voter does not provide ID when they register, they must show ID before voting, vote in person, or include a copy of their ID with their mail-in ballot.

"Voters that have voted in person, or who were imported into VISTA at the time of its creation do not need to show additional ID to vote by mail, but do still need to show valid ID to vote in person," the handbook states.

The state elections office received a complaint from a voter on Monday, according to Deputy Director of Elections Shelly Jackson.

"I think the county just got a little overzealous and marked all the first-time voters" as needing to prove their identity, she said.

Davidson said various reasons led to some voters being incorrectly notified. His office put out a clarification Friday, taking responsibility for the mistake.

"Unfortunately, this notice was also sent to some voters who did not need to provide identification," his office stated. "We recognize that this caused unnecessary confusion, and we sincerely apologize."

The county also included instructions for different types of voters to make sure their ballots are counted:

* **First-time voters:** Follow the identification instructions in your insert if you have not already satisfied the ID requirement.
* **Returning voters:** You do not need to submit additional ID simply because you received this insert.
* **Not sure?** Call our office at **801-851-8683**.

Voters can also sign up to receive alerts on the status of their ballot at vote.utah.gov.

This isn't the first time ballot instructions from Davidson's office have caused confusion. Last year, the county mailed notices instructing voters to include the last four digits of their driver's license, state identification card number or Social Security card number or risk their vote not being counted.

The four-digit requirement is part of a new Utah voter ID law. That provision hasn't taken effect yet, but counties can put a space for those digits on the ballot if they want to.

The issue with incorrect notices being sent appears to be isolated to Utah County.

"I was quite surprised when a couple of voters started contacting our office about this," Jackson said. "It's just not something that we see regularly."

Q: Are voting machines changing Democratic votes to Republican votes? Several posts on Facebook are making that claim.

A: There is no evidence that touchscreen voting machines are deliberately switching voter selections. Rather, elections experts and state election officials have said that reported issues of machines initially not recording votes correctly are a result of familiar machine calibration issues or voter error. Also, nearly the entire country votes in a manner where voters review a paper ballot before having their votes officially cast.

Q: Did the Trump administration have 60 cherry blossom trees cut down in D.C. to build a golf course?

A: In what the Department of Interior called “routine maintenance,” about 60 trees were removed from East Potomac Park, according to the Washington Post. But only one cherry tree removal was mentioned in that article, and an advocacy group opposed to major changes to the park told us it only knew “for certain” of one cherry tree being cut down.

Q: I read this on FB. Is it true? The U.S. Treasury just declared the U.S government is insolvent.

A: No. That’s the conclusion of an opinion piece that cited a Treasury report showing the government’s liabilities outweigh its assets. But that’s been the case for decades, and unlike an insolvent business, the government can levy taxes.

### ICE Officers and Bonuses

Q: Is it true that ICE agents are financially rewarded for the number of people taken into custody?

A: The Department of Homeland Security has said there is no such policy, and an immigration think tank told us it is unaware of any payments per arrest. The Wall Street Journal reported that agents “are rewarded for making arrests” but didn’t say how they are rewarded. Immigration and Customs Enforcement quickly scrapped a proposed program to pay bonuses to speed up deportations.

### Viral Claims About Charlie Kirk’s Words

Since the fatal shooting of Charlie Kirk on Sept. 10, social media users have shared posts showing, quoting or paraphrasing remarks the posts attribute to the conservative activist. Many readers have asked us to provide the facts on whether Kirk, the founder of the youth political group Turning Point USA, made several of these comments.

After the fatal shooting of conservative activist Charlie Kirk, social media claims offering political views of the assassination and the reaction to it quickly spread. Q: Is there an ad in Craigslist to hire people to riot in L.A.?

A: No, there has been no such ad on Craigslist. Some social media posts cited a Craigslist ad to falsely claim it showed that people protesting the immigration raids in Los Angeles were being paid for their actions. But a pair of podcasters told the Associated Press they placed the ad as a prank for their show, and it had nothing to do with the protests.
